Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

worth adjective

worth doing, worth the trouble

also worth it, worthwhile, not worth it, worth seeing, worth the effort, it’s not all that important, not that important, he’s worth nothing, it isn’t worth it, it’s not worth all that, it pays to, it pays to listen, deserving, worthy, deserving of, worthy of

classical

Ter. And. 217: audīreque eōrum est operae pretium audāciam
Plaut. Mil. 31b: nē hercle operae pretium quidemst
Traupman 409: it is worthwhile, operae pretium est; it isn’t worth it, nōn est operae pretium
Traupman 112: nōn est operae pretium
Traupman 105: it pays to listen, pretium operae est auscultāre

operae pretium est

phrase, with an infinitive

it is worth while, worth the trouble

“The pay for the work”; operae pretium facere, to do something worth the effort (Liv. praef. 1).

Other words

  • tantī est — it is worth it (the price, the trouble)

    phrase: genitive of value; nōn est tantī, it isn’t worth it · also used · classical · Cic. Cat. 1.22: sed est tantī, dum modo tua ista sit prīvāta calamitās; Gell. 1.8.6: ego paenitēre tantī nōn emō; Traupman 409: it’s not worth all that, tantī nōn est; Traupman 101: tantī nōn est; Traupman 112: tantī nōn est

  • dignus, digna, dignum — worth (telling, seeing), worthy of

    adjective, with the ablative, a supine in -ū, or quī and the subjunctive · also used · classical · Liv. 4.30.4: nihil dignum dictū āctum hīs cōnsulibus; Ter. Eun. 311: sīve adeō digna rēs est ubi tū nervōs intendās tuōs; Traupman 409: worthy (of), dignus (+ abl); Traupman 151, 159; Traupman 303 · Declension on Wiktionary

    With an infinitive only in verse and post-Augustan prose (Lewis & Short): Horātius ferē sōlus legī dignus, almost the only one worth reading (Quint. 10.1.96).

  • nihil esse — be worth nothing, be a good-for-nothing (of a person)

    also used · classical · Cic. Tusc. 3.77: accēpimus eum nihil hominis esse, a worthless fellow (Lewis & Short s.v. nihil); Traupman 112: nihil est, he’s worth nothing; Traupman 409

    Of a person, “he is nothing”: Latin uses the plain verb where English speaks of worth.

Examples

  • Nē hercle operae pretium quidemst mihi tē narrāre tuās quī virtūtēs sciam.

    Really, it isn’t even worth your telling me of your exploits: I know them already.Plaut. Mil. 31b–32

  • ego paenitēre tantī nōn emō

    I don’t pay that much for something I’ll regretGell. 1.8.6

  • nihil dignum dictū āctum hīs cōnsulibus

    nothing worth telling happened in their yearLiv. 4.30.4

  • Pretium operae est auscultāre.

    It pays to listen.Traupman 105

  • Nōn est pretium operae.

    It’s not worth the trouble.Traupman 398

See also value.
